{{Short description|Informal fallacy}}
{{Italic title}}
An '''''argumentum ad crumenam''''' [[logical argument|argument]], also known as '''an argument to the purse''', is the [[informal fallacy]] of drawing conclusions based on the speaker's financial status.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Fellmeth |first=Aaron X. |title=Guide to Latin in International Law |last2=Horwitz |first2=Maurice |date=2021 |publisher=[[Oxford University Press]] |isbn=9780197583104 |chapter=Argumentum ad crumenam|url=https://www.oxfordreference.com/display/10.1093/acref/9780197583104.001.0001/acref-9780197583104-e-257}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{cite web|url=https://www.logicallyfallacious.com/cgi-bin/uy/webpages.cgi?/logicalfallacies/Argument-to-the-Purse|title=Argument to the Purse|website=Logically Fallacious}}</ref>
The term generally refers to the assumption that having wealth is indicative of insight or virtue, and that poverty denotes the opposite.<ref name=":0" />

The opposite is the ''[[argumentum ad lazarum]]''.

==Examples==
*"If you're so smart, why aren't you rich?"
*"This new law is a good idea. Most of the people against it are riff-raff who make less than $20,000 a year."
*"[[Warren Buffett]] is hosting a seminar. This seminar is better than others, because Warren Buffett is richer than most people."
